nameStory: The species name "leucopodus" comes from Greek meaning "white-footed," referring to the pale coloration of this centipede's legs. The genus name Cryptops means "hidden face" because these centipedes have no visible eyes and seem to navigate their dark underground world by touch alone.
description: The white-footed cave centipede is a slender, worm-like predator that hunts in the dark spaces beneath logs, rocks, and leaf litter. This pale yellowish centipede grows to about 1-2 inches long and has a flattened body with 21 pairs of legs - fewer than many other centipedes. Unlike their faster cousins, these centipedes move with a deliberate, snake-like motion as they search for tiny prey in New England's hidden underground spaces.

idTips.label: Leg count
idTips.description: Always has exactly 21 pairs of legs (42 total) - count carefully as this distinguishes it from other centipede families

idTips.label: Body color
idTips.description: Pale yellowish to cream-colored body that feels smooth and slightly damp to the touch, unlike the harder-bodied soil centipedes

idTips.label: No visible eyes
idTips.description: Head appears completely smooth with no dark eye spots - run your finger gently over the head and you'll feel only smooth, uniform surface

idTips.label: Movement style
idTips.description: Moves in slow, sinuous waves rather than the rapid scurrying of house centipedes - almost snake-like in its deliberate motion

idTips.label: Pale legs
idTips.description: Legs are noticeably lighter in color than the body, appearing almost translucent white or cream - the "white feet" that give it its name

habitat: Found in moist soil under rotting logs, leaf litter, and stones in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. Prefers areas with rich, dark humus soil that stays consistently damp, often near streams or in sheltered valleys. Look in the same spots where you'd find salamanders - they share similar moisture requirements.

seasonality.spring: Most active as soil warms and becomes workable again. Look under logs and stones that have stayed moist through snowmelt - they'll be closer to the surface now.
seasonality.summer: Moves deeper into soil during hot, dry periods but can still be found under consistently moist logs and deep leaf litter in shaded areas.
seasonality.fall: Active again as temperatures cool and autumn rains return moisture to upper soil layers. Good time to search as they hunt for overwintering prey.
seasonality.winter: Inactive deep in soil below frost line, essentially impossible to find without major digging in frozen ground.

funFact: Despite being completely blind, white-footed cave centipedes can catch and subdue prey in total darkness using specialized sensory hairs that detect the tiniest vibrations - they can sense a small insect moving from several inches away through soil particles alone.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Common Cryptops, but white-footed cave centipedes are noticeably paler overall with more contrasting light-colored legs. Remember: "White feet, white treat" - if the legs stand out as much lighter than the body, you've found the white-footed species.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertain claim flag**: This species has only been recorded once in New England, so much of the habitat and seasonal information is extrapolated from related species and general centipede biology. If you think you've found one, consider photographing it for local naturalists to verify.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative Common Cryptops, the white-footed cave centipede is generally paler throughout with more pronounced light-colored legs that contrast sharply with the body. Common Cryptops tends to be more uniformly colored without the distinct "white socks" appearance. Both share the same 21-pair leg count and eyeless head, but the color difference is usually reliable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common Cryptops can be distinguished from its close relative Cryptops leucopodus by its more golden-brown coloration, whereas leucopodus tends to be paler and more yellowish.
